title: SpaceX Launches 6,300‑lb Cargo to ISS Today – Watch Live Stream Now!
body:
A SpaceX Falcon 9 is set to blast off from Cape Canaveral at 6:33 a.m. Eastern Time on October 13, carrying a Dragon cargo spacecraft loaded with roughly 6,300 pounds (2,860 kilograms) of scientific equipment, supplies and hardware for the International Space Station. The mission, designated CRS‑28, marks the company’s 28th resupply flight under NASA’s Commercial Resupply Services contract and will be streamed live for the public to watch as the rocket climbs toward low‑Earth orbit.

The payload manifests a diverse mix of experiments that will occupy the station’s laboratory modules for months to come. Among the cargo are several new biology studies slated to investigate how microgravity influences cellular processes, a set of materials‑science samples that will test the durability of next‑generation alloys, and a suite of Earth‑observation instruments intended to improve climate‑monitoring capabilities. In addition, the flight carries a fresh batch of food, clothing, and personal items for the crew, as well as spare parts for the station’s life‑support and power systems. The cargo manifest also includes a new “space‑based 3‑D printer” that NASA hopes will demonstrate on‑orbit manufacturing of replacement components, a technology that could reduce dependence on costly launch deliveries in the future.

SpaceX’s Dragon capsule, now on its 28th mission, is the only spacecraft capable of returning sizable payloads from the ISS to Earth. After a roughly 24‑hour rendezvous with the station, the uncrewed vehicle will be grappled by the station’s robotic arm and berthed to the Harmony module. Over the following days, astronauts will unload the supplies, install experiments, and load the capsule with about 4,000 pounds of research results, hardware slated for refurbishment, and other items destined for analysis back on the ground. The Dragon will then detach and perform a controlled re‑entry, splashing down in the Pacific Ocean where recovery teams will retrieve the cargo for transport to NASA’s processing facilities.

The CRS‑28 launch underscores the growing reliance on commercial partners for the day‑to‑day operation of the orbiting laboratory. Since 2012, SpaceX has completed more than 20 resupply missions, consistently achieving a high success rate and delivering cargo on a schedule that aligns with the station’s rotating crew rotations. The partnership has also enabled NASA to focus its resources on deep‑space exploration initiatives, such as the Artemis program and the upcoming Europa Clipper mission, while still maintaining a robust presence in low‑Earth orbit. Moreover, the frequent cadence of Dragon flights provides a valuable testbed for new technologies, including autonomous docking procedures and advanced thermal‑control systems that could be adapted for future crewed spacecraft.

Beyond the immediate logistical benefits, the mission carries strategic importance for the United States’ leadership in space. The ability to launch, service, and return cargo reliably supports a wide array of scientific research that can inform everything from medical breakthroughs to climate policy. It also demonstrates the viability of a commercial supply chain that could be replicated for lunar gateway stations or Martian outposts. As the space economy expands, the data gathered from each cargo flight feeds into a broader ecosystem of private‑sector innovation, encouraging competition and driving down costs for future missions.

Looking ahead, the successful execution of CRS‑28 will set the stage for the next phase of NASA’s partnership with SpaceX, which includes the upcoming cargo missions under the new CRS‑2 contract and the company’s crewed Crew‑Dragon flights that ferry astronauts to and from the ISS. As the station approaches the end of its current operational life in the late 2020s, the experience gained from these resupply operations will be instrumental in shaping the logistics architecture for the next generation of orbital habitats and deep‑space exploration platforms. The launch this morning, therefore, is not just a routine delivery—it is a stepping stone toward a more sustainable and versatile presence beyond Earth.
